gains.title: Fewer stoppages
gains.short: Every stoppage counted, even the shortest.
gains.body: Every stoppage is recorded, even the shortest, with its duration and its time. The ones nobody wrote down appear, add up, and you finally know where production is lost.
gains.alt: A production day on which short stoppages appear one by one, then add up to a clearly visible loss of time.

gains.title: Less wasted energy
gains.short: What runs for nothing, finally visible.
gains.body: What consumes outside production becomes visible: machines running at night, leaks, standby modes that are not. You stop paying for an empty shop floor.
gains.alt: Several days of consumption: at night the curve does not drop back to standby level, and the gap, every night, is wasted energy.

gains.title: Decisions based on facts
gains.body: Indicators are calculated from the machines, not rebuilt by hand. You know what improves and what slips, and you decide on figures rather than impressions.
gains.alt: An indicator tracked week after week: the bars rise, the trend is drawn and an arrow confirms the improvement.

meta.title: Protocols · Thirteen industrial protocols included · Meshvise
meta.description: Modbus TCP and RTU, OPC UA, BACnet/IP, Siemens S7, MQTT, EtherNet/IP, Beckhoff ADS, REST, WebSocket, Webhook, Sparkplug B, MTConnect. Transport, addressing, direction and covered equipment for each.

hero.title: Thirteen protocols, one engine
hero.subtitle: Every protocol is a driver of the same acquisition engine. All are included in the licence: no module to buy per PLC brand, no option to enable.

missing.title: What is not supported
missing.intro: Saying what is missing avoids a commissioning that goes wrong. These protocols are not implemented today and are not publicly dated.
items: IEC 60870-5 and IEC 61850, for substations and power distribution.
DNP3, for water and North American utility networks.
M-Bus and wireless M-Bus, for sub-metering.
PROFINET and EtherCAT in direct access. Those PLCs generally expose OPC UA or Modbus TCP, both supported.
missing.ask: Missing a protocol? Write in, the list follows real requests.

proprietary.title: Machine tools and proprietary protocols
proprietary.intro: Numerical controls and some PLCs speak a house protocol, tied to a licensed library the vendor is not allowed to redistribute. No supervision system connects to it directly without going through the manufacturer, and the option that opens the machine is expensive, usually billed per machine. So the right question is not "do you support Fanuc" but "what do I need to measure, and at what price".
proprietary.principle: Meshvise does not replace the manufacturer's gateway, it connects to its standardised output. As soon as a machine exposes OPC UA, MQTT or Modbus, it becomes equipment like any other.
proprietary.ladder_title: Four routes, from the cheapest to the most expensive
proprietary.ladder_intro: The option that makes a machine speak a standard protocol is almost always paid for, billed per machine, and sometimes bundled with a control upgrade. A quote like that is enough to bury a project. Yet there are three cheaper routes before that one, and they cover most indicators.
proprietary.ladder_key: Tracking how a machine runs does not require reading its numerical control. Running, stopped, cycle and parts produced can be measured from the outside, for a fraction of the price of a manufacturer option.

ladder_rows.gets: Running, stopped, fault, cycle end, depending on what the machine already exposes on terminals.
ladder_rows.when: Always look here first. Many machines expose unused dry contacts that a small Modbus input module reads for the price of a cabinet component.

ladder_rows.gets: Consumption, spindle current, cycle time, part counting, downtime, stack light state.
ladder_rows.cost: A few hundred euros per machine
ladder_rows.when: The best value for money when the machine is closed or old. A current clamp and a communicating energy meter are enough to see a machine run, timestamp its stops and measure its consumption.

ladder_rows.gets: The control's process data, translated into OPC UA, MQTT or MTConnect.
ladder_rows.cost: Varies, often less than the manufacturer option
ladder_rows.when: When you need internal variables: running program, override, machine alarms, dimensions. Adds equipment to maintain, but stays useful even if you change supervision.

ladder_rows.gets: Everything the control exposes, with no intermediary, backed by the manufacturer.
ladder_rows.when: On a new machine, where the option is negotiated at order time and costs far less than added afterwards. On an existing fleet, keep it for critical machines.

proprietary.ladder_advice: On a fleet of several machines, what works is equipping the whole fleet from the bottom of the ladder to finally see the whole picture, then going deeper on the two or three machines that really carry performance.

rows.route: OPC UA option on recent controls, an MTConnect agent read directly, otherwise a FOCAS gateway to OPC UA or MQTT.
rows.note: The FOCAS library is licensed by Fanuc and is not redistributable: nobody can embed it in their product. Check whether the OPC UA option is already enabled, it sometimes is without anyone knowing. If it has to be bought, compare its quote with the first two routes of the ladder before deciding.

rows.route: Modbus TCP communication module, OPC UA module on recent ranges, or an SLMP gateway to MQTT.
rows.note: Many MELSEC installations already expose Modbus TCP through a rack module: look in the cabinet before buying anything. A second-hand communication module costs a fraction of a software option.

rows.route: EtherNet/IP or Modbus TCP, both supported directly.
rows.note: Recent ranges speak EtherNet/IP natively, which removes the question entirely.
The proprietary protocol is mostly for programming. To read values, Modbus is enough and it is present everywhere.

rows.route: MTConnect or OPC UA depending on the generation, both read directly.
rows.note: On a machine built after 2015, the question to ask the manufacturer is: can the machine output OPC UA or MTConnect, and under what conditions.

proprietary.gateway_title: What a gateway changes, and what it does not
proprietary.gateway_body: A gateway translates the manufacturer's protocol into an open one. It adds equipment to maintain and a point of failure, but it makes the machine readable by any system, not only by Meshvise. That investment stays valid if you change supervision.
proprietary.mtconnect: MTConnect has been read directly since September 2026: Meshvise queries the agent as a client, which yields the running program, the execution state and the part count without going through a cell PLC. The manufacturer's agent remains an installation prerequisite.

opcua_security.title: OPC UA security, in plain terms
opcua_security.intro: This is not a refinement, it is a condition of access. A Siemens PLC of the 1500 range ships configured to sign or encrypt its exchanges, and refuses an unprotected session. Without this, a site equipped that way simply cannot be connected.

rows.note: The Basic128Rsa15 and Basic256 policies are not offered: they are deprecated by the OPC Foundation and cryptographically broken. The underlying library still exposes them, Meshvise does not carry them over.

rows.value: None, sign only, or sign and encrypt.
rows.note: Signing proves the origin and integrity of messages. Encrypting adds confidentiality. The mode is chosen according to what the server requires.

rows.value: Username and password, independent of encryption.
rows.note: The standard keeps both settings separate: a server may require an account without encrypting the channel, or the reverse. Meshvise follows that separation instead of imposing one.

rows.value: Explicit verification, enabled by providing the certificate.
rows.note: With no certificate provided, Meshvise accepts whatever the server presents and says so, in the driver log and on screen. That is trust on first use, defensible only on a closed shop-floor network.

opcua_security.strict: An incomplete security configuration is rejected at three levels: in the database, in the driver and in the form. There is no silent fallback to a cleartext session: either the connection matches what you asked for, or it fails with a message.

how.title: How a point is configured
how.body: A driver carries the connection: address, port, credentials, cadence. Each point carries its address within the protocol, its data type and its unit. Compatible equipment is discovered automatically where the protocol allows it, otherwise configuration is done by import or by hand. One site mixes as many protocols as needed in a single instance.

list.name: Modbus TCP
list.desc: The most widespread industrial standard. Reads holding registers and coils, writes register by register or bit by bit. Read batches are split automatically below the 125-register limit set by the protocol.
list.equipment: PLCs, variable-speed drives, energy meters, controllers, sensors behind a gateway
list.note: Range splitting and slave unit handling are automatic.

list.name: Modbus RTU
list.desc: The same protocol over serial, with the same read and write surface. The connection goes through a serial-to-TCP converter, common and inexpensive hardware.
list.equipment: Sub-meters, older sensors, drives on a fieldbus
list.note: Plan a serial-to-Ethernet converter; baud rate, parity and stop bits are set in the driver.

list.name: OPC UA
list.desc: The only protocol here that does not poll. Meshvise creates a real subscription on the server and registers every point as a monitored item. The server pushes the value when it changes. No wasted reads on stable values, and a latency that follows the equipment rather than a chosen cadence. The channel can be secured: signing or encryption, a user account, verification of the server certificate.
list.equipment: Recent PLCs, machine tools, third-party systems exposing an OPC UA server
list.note: Three encryption policies are offered, the ones the OPC Foundation still recommends. The two older ones, cryptographically broken, are deliberately not offered even though the library exposes them. An incomplete configuration is rejected rather than degraded: never a silent fallback to a cleartext session.

list.name: BACnet/IP
list.desc: The protocol of buildings and HVAC. Reads analogue, binary and multi-state objects with their presence and value properties.
list.equipment: Air handling units, boilers, zone controllers, commercial metering, chillers
list.note: Broadcast discovery is not used: equipment is declared by address, which avoids surprises on segmented networks and in containers.

list.name: Siemens S7
list.desc: Direct access to Siemens PLCs without an intermediate server. Each point lives at a precise position inside a data block: block number, byte offset and data type.
list.note: On the 1200 and 1500 ranges, optimised block access must be disabled on the PLC, or the block declared accessible.

list.name: MQTT
list.desc: Versions 3.1.1 and 5.0. Meshvise subscribes to the declared topics and keeps the latest value of each. When the payload is a JSON object, a dotted path selects the value to extract, for example data.temperature.
list.equipment: Wireless sensors, field gateways, existing brokers, industrial connected devices
list.note: Works with an existing broker: Meshvise connects as a client, it does not impose its own.

list.name: EtherNet/IP
list.desc: The protocol of Rockwell PLCs, with symbolic addressing. A point declares the tag name inside the controller directly, using program and array syntax.
list.equipment: ControlLogix L7 and L8 series, CompactLogix L1 to L3 series
list.note: Program-scoped tags and structure members are reachable with their native notation.

list.name: Beckhoff ADS
list.desc: Access to TwinCAT runtimes by naming program variables directly, for example a speed variable in the main block or a boolean in a global list.
list.equipment: CX embedded controllers, industrial PCs running TwinCAT 2 or 3
list.note: The variable type is declared explicitly: the protocol does not expose it automatically. Two numbers not to be confused: the connection goes through the AMS router on TCP port 48898, whereas the AMS port designates the runtime being queried, 851 for TwinCAT 3 and 801 for TwinCAT 2.

list.name: REST
list.desc: Periodic polling of any HTTP interface returning JSON. Authentication by username and password or by token. Writing goes back through the same interface.
list.equipment: Business systems, weather stations, inverters, third-party services, proprietary gateways
list.note: Useful to pull in a source that is not industrial at all but counts in an indicator.

list.name: WebSocket
list.desc: Permanent connection to a service that pushes its values. Every incoming message is parsed as JSON and feeds the point cache.
list.equipment: Equipment or services broadcasting a proprietary real-time stream
list.note: The connection re-establishes itself after a drop.

list.name: Webhook
list.desc: The inverse of the REST driver. Meshvise exposes an address and waits for the remote system to publish its values there. Useful when the source refuses to be polled or is only reachable outbound.
list.equipment: Third-party platforms, LoRa sensors through their network server, notification services
list.note: Read-only by construction: Meshvise is the server in this direction.

list.name: Sparkplug B
list.desc: Standardised industrial MQTT. Meshvise acts as the host application, the supervisor role: it reads birth messages to build the metric table, then decodes the data messages. A write goes out as a command message, to the node or the device. Equipment structure is discovered, not declared.
list.note: Automatic metric discovery is the main benefit: plugging in a gateway is enough for its points to appear.

list.name: MTConnect
list.desc: The de facto standard of the machine tool world, native on Haas, Mazak, Okuma and Doosan, available on Fanuc and Siemens through a manufacturer's adapter. Meshvise queries the agent as a client: the probe discovers the points, current state is polled at the chosen rate. The running program, execution state, part count and spindle load are read directly, without going through a cell PLC.
list.equipment: Machining centres, CNC lathes, machines fitted with an MTConnect agent
list.note: The standard is a three-tier architecture: the machine talks to an adapter, the adapter to an agent, the agent to Meshvise. The agent is therefore an installation prerequisite, stated in the quote; most recent controls ship with one. Read-only by nature: no agent accepts a write, and commanding a machine tool goes through its own numerical control.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.subtitle: If yours is not here, write to contact@meshvise.com.

hardware.a: Two cores, four gigabytes of memory, twenty gigabytes of disk for five hundred points and thirty days of history. A shop-floor mini-PC or an existing server is enough.

disappear.a: Your data stays on your server, in a standard database, readable without Meshvise. Any integrator can take over operations.

notfor.a: Very large multi-country groups with twelve-month buying cycles, projects under fifty points, and anything that falls under functional safety.

support.a: By email, reply within two business days, from the person who wrote the code.

updates.a: Yes, every one released during the subscription, fixes and major versions alike. No separate maintenance contract, no upgrade fee. Only help with a migration is billed, as time spent.

trial_how.a: You describe your site in the contact form, choosing "Trial on your equipment". We send you a quote that sets the duration, the scope and the support. The trial then runs on your infrastructure, with your equipment.

demo_vs_trial.q: What is the difference between the demo and the trial?
demo_vs_trial.a: The demo is public and runs on a simulated site, nothing to install. The trial runs on your premises, on your real equipment.

privacy.lede: The website collects one thing only: what you write in the contact form. Here is what happens to it.

sections.title: Data controller
body: {nom}, publisher of the website, reachable at {email}. Full contact details are in the {legal}.

sections.title: Data collected
body: The contact form collects your name, your company, your email address, the subject of your request and the message you write. Nothing is collected until you send it.
As with any website, the host processes each visitor's IP address to deliver the pages and protect the site, in particular to limit repeated submissions of the form.

sections.title: Purpose and legal basis
body: This data serves one purpose: answering your request, whether it concerns a licence, a trial, a demonstration or a question. Processing relies on pre-contractual steps taken at your request (Article 6(1)(b) GDPR) and, for a general question, on the legitimate interest in answering you (Article 6(1)(f)).
It is neither sold nor transferred, and is used for no mailing you did not ask for.

sections.title: Recipients
body: Your request is read by the publisher only. To deliver it, three providers process it on the publisher's behalf: Cloudflare, which hosts the website, Resend, which sends the email, and Google, which provides the mailbox that receives it.
These three companies are established in the United States. Data transfers to them are governed by the EU-US Data Privacy Framework or by the European Commission's standard contractual clauses.

sections.title: Retention
body: Your data is kept for three years after the last exchange, then deleted. If your request leads to a contract, the data it needs is kept for the duration of the contract, then for as long as accounting obligations require.

sections.title: Cookies
body: The website sets no cookie of its own and uses no audience measurement, advertising or social media tool: no banner asks for your consent. Cloudflare may set a technical security cookie, strictly necessary to the service and exempt from consent.

sections.title: Your rights
body: You can access your data, have it corrected or erased, object to its processing, or ask for its restriction or portability, by writing to {email}. You will receive an answer within one month.
If you believe your rights are not respected, you can lodge a complaint with the CNIL, the French data protection authority, {cnil}.
